subChunks.title: Exploring the Dataset: Descriptives & Correlations
subChunks.hookHtml: A research team has collected data from 120 university students across three year groups (first, second, and final year) measuring academic burnout, perceived social support, sleep quality, and academic engagement. The data are now in your hands. Before you test a single hypothesis, you need to understand what the data look like — their shape, spread, and inter-relationships. The two most common errors in psychological data analysis are testing hypotheses before exploring the data (missing outliers, violations, and unexpected patterns) and reporting means without context. This sub-chunk is where real analysis always begins.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Capstone Dataset

The dataset capstone_data contains 120 observations across five variables:

  • burnout — Academic burnout score (Maslach Burnout Inventory – Student Survey, MBI-SS; 0–6 scale; higher = more burned out)
  • support — Perceived social support (Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support, MSPSS; 1–7 scale; higher = more support)
  • sleep — Sleep problems (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, PSQI total; 0–21; higher = worse sleep quality)
  • engage — Academic engagement (Utrecht Work Engagement Scale – Student version, UWES-S; 0–6; higher = more engaged)
  • cohort — Year group: "First", "Second", or "Final" (balanced, n = 40 per group)

Research questions: (1) Does burnout differ significantly across year groups? (2) Do social support and sleep quality independently predict burnout? You will answer these in 4b. First, understand the data.

Inspecting a Data Frame

str(capstone_data)          # variable types and first few values
head(capstone_data)         # first 6 rows
dim(capstone_data)          # rows × columns: 120 × 5
summary(capstone_data)      # min, quartiles, mean, max for each variable

summary() is your first diagnostic: check for implausible values (burnout < 0, sleep > 21), NAs, and whether factor levels look correct.

Group Descriptives with tapply()

To compute a statistic separately for each level of a factor, use tapply() (table apply):

tapply(capstone_data$burnout, capstone_data$cohort, mean)   # mean by cohort
tapply(capstone_data$burnout, capstone_data$cohort, sd)     # SD by cohort

This returns a named vector: one value per factor level. In a publication, you would report M and SD for each group before running any inferential test.

Correlation Matrix

A correlation matrix shows Pearson's r for every pair of continuous variables simultaneously:

cor(capstone_data[, c("burnout", "support", "sleep", "engage")])

The matrix is symmetric around a diagonal of 1s (each variable correlated with itself). Check: do the correlations make theoretical sense? You would expect burnout to correlate negatively with support and engagement, and positively with sleep problems. Correlations that contradict your hypotheses before testing are a flag to investigate — not to ignore. round(cor(...), 2) formats to two decimal places for readability.

Why Explore Before Testing?

Data exploration protects against four common pitfalls: (1) outliers that disproportionately influence means and correlations; (2) distributional violations that affect the validity of parametric tests; (3) unexpected patterns (e.g., a non-linear relationship) that a linear model will miss; and (4) data quality issues (impossible values, misrecorded data, wrong factor levels). Exploratory analysis should be documented and reported — not treated as a hidden precursor to the 'real' analysis. The distinction between exploratory and confirmatory analysis must be preserved and declared.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen opens the capstone dataset. 'We have 120 students, five variables, three year groups. Before we ask whether burnout differs by year, we need to know: what does the burnout distribution look like? Are there outliers? Does the pattern of correlations make sense?'

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: str(capstone_data). Confirms the structure: 120 observations, five variables, cohort is a three-level factor. summary(capstone_data). Burnout ranges from near 0 to about 5.5 — within the 0-6 scale, no impossible values. Sleep ranges from 3 to 18 — plausible. Good data hygiene confirmed before we proceed.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: tapply(capstone_data$burnout, capstone_data$cohort, mean). First-year mean ≈ 2.50, second-year ≈ 2.21, final-year ≈ 2.91. The pattern is interesting: second-year students have the lowest burnout, final-year the highest. Is that difference significant? That is what 4b answers.
She computes the correlation matrix. Burnout correlates at r ≈ −0.50 with support and r ≈ +0.45 with sleep problems. Both in the predicted directions.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: The correlations are moderate-to-strong and theoretically coherent. If burnout had correlated positively with support, that would be our first clue that something was wrong with the data or the construct measurement — before we'd run a single inferential test. Exploration is not a luxury. It is how you avoid publishing nonsense.

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Independent Practice — From Scratch

The same capstone_data is loaded. Without starter code, write R that produces all four variables: burnout_mean, burnout_sd, group_means, and cor_matrix. All five test cases must pass.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: A colleague says "I always just run the analysis straight away — the results section is all that matters." Explain what could go wrong if you skip the data exploration phase, using two specific examples from the capstone dataset context.

rabbitHoleTerms.definition: R's table-apply function: applies a function to subsets of a vector defined by a factor. tapply(x, group, FUN) returns a named vector with one result per factor level — the standard way to compute group descriptive statistics before an ANOVA.

The Maslach Burnout Inventory – Student Survey, a validated 15-item scale measuring academic burnout on three dimensions: exhaustion, cynicism, and academic efficacy. The composite score ranges 0–6; higher scores indicate greater burnout. Widely used in educational psychology research.

A critical distinction: confirmatory analysis tests pre-specified hypotheses against a significance criterion; exploratory analysis searches for patterns without prior prediction. Results from exploratory analysis must be clearly labelled as such and cannot be interpreted with the same inferential weight as confirmatory tests — and require independent confirmation.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher computing a correlation matrix finds that burnout correlates positively with support (r = +0.38, p = .001) — opposite to the predicted direction. Before concluding that social support increases burnout, what should the researcher do first?
options: Report the finding as a novel discovery; unexpected results are more publishable
Check for data entry errors, verify scale scoring direction, and inspect whether the sample is unusually high-scoring on support
Re-code the support scale so that higher scores mean less support, to produce the expected negative correlation
Exclude the 10 participants with the highest support scores and re-run the correlation
questions.correctAnswer: Check for data entry errors, verify scale scoring direction, and inspect whether the sample is unusually high-scoring on support
questions.explanationHtml: A correlation opposite to the predicted direction is a data quality signal before it is a theoretical result. The most common causes are scale scoring errors (a higher score was mistakenly treated as worse rather than better, or vice versa), data entry errors, or a mismatched variable. Only after ruling out these methodological explanations should the researcher consider theoretical interpretations of an unexpected finding — and even then, an unreplicated counter-theoretical correlation requires cautious, tentative interpretation.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: In R, cor(capstone_data) will compute Pearson correlations for all variables in the data frame, including the factor variable cohort.
questions.explanationHtml: cor() requires all inputs to be numeric. If the data frame includes a factor variable (such as cohort), R will either return an error or coerce the factor to numeric in a way that produces meaningless correlations (treating factor level codes as a numeric scale). The correct approach is to select only the continuous numeric variables: cor(capstone_data[, c("burnout", "support", "sleep", "engage")]).

questions.questionHtml: A student computes group means with tapply() and finds: First = 2.50, Second = 2.21, Final = 2.91. They immediately conclude that final-year students have significantly higher burnout. What methodological error are they making?
options: They are using the wrong function — aggregate() should be used instead of tapply()

They are treating descriptive statistics (sample means) as if they were inferential results — group means always differ by chance; only a significance test can establish whether the differences exceed sampling error
The group means cannot be compared because the groups are not balanced in size
Burnout is an ordinal variable and cannot be compared using means
questions.correctAnswer: They are treating descriptive statistics (sample means) as if they were inferential results — group means always differ by chance; only a significance test can establish whether the differences exceed sampling error
questions.explanationHtml: Descriptive statistics describe the sample; inferential statistics make claims about the population from which the sample was drawn. Sample means will always differ to some degree due to random sampling variation — even if the true population means are identical. A significance test (here, ANOVA) determines whether the observed group differences are large enough, relative to within-group variability, to be distinguished from chance. Computing descriptive statistics is a necessary precursor to inferential testing, not a substitute for it.

questions.questionHtml: Which R function provides a rapid initial data overview including min, max, quartiles, mean, and the number of NAs for each variable in a data frame?
options: str()
summary()
describe()
head()
questions.explanationHtml: summary() applied to a data frame returns a statistical overview for each column: minimum, 1st quartile, median, mean, 3rd quartile, and maximum for numeric variables, plus the count of NAs. For factors, it shows the count per level. str() shows data types and the first few values but not statistics. head() shows the first six rows. describe() is from the Hmisc package and is not in base R.

subChunks.title: Testing Hypotheses: ANOVA & Multiple Regression
subChunks.hookHtml: You have explored the data. The group means suggest final-year students have the highest burnout; the correlation matrix indicates that social support and sleep quality are both associated with burnout in the expected directions. Now you test whether these patterns are statistically significant and estimate their magnitude. Two analyses are needed: a one-way ANOVA to determine whether burnout differs across year groups, and a multiple regression to examine whether social support and sleep quality independently predict burnout when considered together. Multiple regression — using more than one predictor simultaneously — is essential here, because support and sleep may themselves be correlated; controlling for one while estimating the other gives a cleaner picture of each predictor's unique contribution.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Multiple Regression

Multiple regression extends simple regression to include two or more predictors simultaneously:

burnout = b₀ + b₁ × support + b₂ × sleep + ε

Each slope (b₁, b₂) represents the unique contribution of that predictor to the outcome, controlling for all other predictors in the model. This is the central advantage over running two separate simple regressions: a predictor may appear significant in isolation but non-significant (or even change direction) when shared variance with another predictor is accounted for.

reg_model <- lm(burnout ~ support + sleep, data = capstone_data)
summary(reg_model)

The summary output for multiple regression adds an adjusted R² (R²_adj) alongside R²: it penalises for the number of predictors in the model to prevent inflation from adding uninformative variables. Always report adjusted R² in multiple regression.

Model Comparison

A key question in multiple regression is whether adding a second predictor significantly improves the model over a simpler one. Compare models using anova():

model1 <- lm(burnout ~ support, data = capstone_data)
model2 <- lm(burnout ~ support + sleep, data = capstone_data)
anova(model1, model2)   # F-test for the improvement in fit

A significant F in this comparison confirms that sleep quality adds explanatory power beyond what social support alone provides.

Checking Regression Assumptions

plot(reg_model)   # four diagnostic plots

Plot 1 (Residuals vs Fitted): should show random scatter around y = 0 — no systematic pattern. A curve indicates non-linearity. Plot 2 (Q-Q): residuals should fall on the diagonal line — departures indicate non-normality. Plot 3 (Scale-Location): the spread of residuals should be constant across fitted values (homoscedasticity). Plot 4 (Cook's Distance): identifies influential observations; points labelled by row number warrant investigation.

Extracting APA Values from R Output

summary(reg_model)$r.squared        # R²
summary(reg_model)$adj.r.squared    # adjusted R²
summary(reg_model)$fstatistic       # F, df1, df2
coef(summary(reg_model))            # full coefficient table

For a complete APA results section you need: unstandardised coefficients (b), standard errors (SE), t-values, p-values, and 95% CIs for each predictor; R² and adjusted R²; overall F with both df values and p. Standardised coefficients (β, computed by running the analysis on z-scored variables) are often reported alongside b to allow comparison of effect magnitudes across predictors on different scales.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen moves to the inferential phase. 'We have two questions. First: does burnout differ across year groups? That's a one-way ANOVA — we've done this in 3f. Second: do support and sleep independently predict burnout? That's multiple regression.'

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: anova_model <- aov(burnout ~ cohort, data = capstone_data). summary(anova_model). The F-statistic is large and p << .001. There are significant burnout differences across year groups. TukeyHSD tells us all three pairwise comparisons are significant: second-year students have significantly lower burnout than first, and final-year students have significantly higher burnout than both.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Now multiple regression. reg_model <- lm(burnout ~ support + sleep, data = capstone_data). Both predictors are significant. Support: b = −0.27, meaning each additional point of social support predicts a 0.27-point drop in burnout, holding sleep constant. Sleep: b = 0.08, meaning each additional PSQI point predicts a 0.08-point rise in burnout, holding support constant.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Adjusted R² ≈ 0.32 — support and sleep together explain about 32% of variance in burnout. That is substantial for a two-predictor model in real psychological data. In 4c you will write this up in APA format. The key skill is translating R output into sentences a reader without R can evaluate.

Independent Practice — From Scratch

The same capstone_data is loaded. Without starter code, write R that produces: anova_model (ANOVA), tukey_result (Tukey HSD), eta_sq (eta-squared), reg_model (multiple regression), and r_sq_adj (adjusted R²). All five test cases must pass.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a postgraduate student who has only ever run simple regression why you need multiple regression when investigating both social support and sleep quality as predictors of burnout. What does "controlling for" another variable actually mean, and why does it matter?

rabbitHoleTerms.definition: A penalised version of R² that accounts for the number of predictors in the model. Adding any predictor to a regression model — even a useless one — increases R² slightly; adjusted R² corrects for this by applying a penalty proportional to the number of predictors relative to sample size. Always prefer adjusted R² in multiple regression.

When two or more predictors in a multiple regression model are strongly correlated with each other. High multicollinearity inflates standard errors of regression coefficients, making estimates unstable and difficult to interpret. Detected via Variance Inflation Factor (VIF): VIF > 10 indicates a serious problem.

A predictor that appears non-significant in simple regression but becomes significant (or increases in magnitude) in multiple regression because its inclusion 'suppresses' variance in another predictor that is irrelevant to the outcome. An example of why simple and multiple regression results can diverge dramatically.

A measure of each observation's influence on all regression coefficients simultaneously. Points with Cook's D > 4/n (a common rule of thumb) are potentially influential outliers that warrant investigation — not automatic exclusion, but careful examination.

questions.questionHtml: In the multiple regression lm(burnout ~ support + sleep), the coefficient for support is b = −0.27, p < .001. In a simple regression lm(burnout ~ support), the coefficient is b = −0.31, p < .001. Which interpretation of the difference is most accurate?
options: The multiple regression coefficient is incorrect because support was more strongly associated with burnout in simple regression

In multiple regression, b = −0.27 represents the unique contribution of support to burnout after removing the shared variance with sleep quality; the slight attenuation reflects that sleep quality accounts for some of the association seen in simple regression
The difference is due to rounding error and the two coefficients should be treated as identical
Simple regression is always more accurate than multiple regression for testing the effect of a single predictor
questions.correctAnswer: In multiple regression, b = −0.27 represents the unique contribution of support to burnout after removing the shared variance with sleep quality; the slight attenuation reflects that sleep quality accounts for some of the association seen in simple regression
questions.explanationHtml: In multiple regression, each coefficient represents the unique effect of that predictor after holding all other predictors constant. Because support and sleep quality are likely correlated (students with poor sleep may also have weaker support networks), some of the apparent association between support and burnout in simple regression reflects shared variance with sleep. The multiple regression coefficient of −0.27 is a more precise estimate of support's specific contribution, independent of sleep. This is why multiple regression is preferred when multiple related predictors are involved.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: Adding more predictors to a multiple regression model will always increase the adjusted R-squared, making larger models automatically preferable.
questions.explanationHtml: Regular R² increases monotonically with additional predictors (it can only increase or stay the same, never decrease). Adjusted R² does not: it penalises for additional predictors and will decrease if a predictor is added that explains less variance than the penalty incurred. This is why adjusted R² is preferred for comparing models with different numbers of predictors — it rewards parsimony and prevents overfitting.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher runs the capstone regression and finds that the Residuals vs Fitted plot shows a clear U-shaped curve, with residuals negative at low fitted values, near zero in the middle, and positive at high fitted values. What does this indicate?
options: The residuals are normally distributed — the U-shape is expected
There is heteroscedasticity — the variance of residuals changes across fitted values
There is a non-linear relationship between one or more predictors and the outcome that the linear model is not capturing
There are influential outliers at the extreme ends of the burnout scale
questions.correctAnswer: There is a non-linear relationship between one or more predictors and the outcome that the linear model is not capturing
questions.explanationHtml: The Residuals vs Fitted plot should show random scatter around y = 0 if the linearity assumption is met. A systematic U-shape (negative residuals at low fitted values, positive at high) indicates that the model consistently under-predicts at the extremes and over-predicts in the middle — the signature of a non-linear relationship that the linear model cannot capture. The appropriate remedies include transforming a predictor, adding a polynomial term (x²), or fitting a non-linear model. Heteroscedasticity produces a fan shape (widening variance), not a U-shape.

questions.questionHtml: Which R function allows you to formally compare two nested regression models (e.g., a model with one predictor vs a model with two predictors) to determine whether the additional predictor significantly improves fit?
options: compare(model1, model2)
anova(model1, model2)
summary(model2) vs summary(model1)
TukeyHSD(model1, model2)
questions.explanationHtml: anova(model1, model2) performs an F-test comparing the fit of two nested regression models — where model1's predictors are a subset of model2's. The F-statistic tests whether the reduction in residual sum of squares from model1 to model2 is larger than expected by chance. A significant F (p < .05) indicates that the additional predictor(s) in model2 significantly improve prediction. This is the standard approach to incremental validity testing in hierarchical multiple regression.

subChunks.title: Interpreting & Writing Up: The APA Results Section
subChunks.hookHtml: You have run the analyses. R has produced numbers. Now comes the hardest part: translating those numbers into prose that a reader without R — a clinician, a policy-maker, a peer reviewer — can evaluate. The results section of a psychology paper is not a list of statistics; it is an argument from evidence. Each number carries an interpretation, and the interpretation must be explicitly stated. This sub-chunk gives you the R console outputs from the capstone analyses and asks you to write a complete, publication-ready APA 7 results section — then critically evaluate what the findings do and do not establish.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Structure of an APA Results Section

A well-structured results section moves in a principled sequence:

  1. Preliminary analyses: descriptive statistics (M, SD) for all key variables; inter-correlations; any assumption checks that required action.
  2. Primary analyses: each inferential test, in the order they were pre-specified. Report the test statistic, df, p-value, and effect size for every test.
  3. Post-hoc analyses: if ANOVA is significant, Tukey results; if regression has multiple predictors, report each coefficient.

What the results section does not do: interpret, explain, theorise, or compare to other studies. That is the Discussion section's role. The results section states what the data show; the discussion explains what it means.

The Capstone Results (from R output)

The analyses from 4a and 4b yielded the following (use these values in your guided practice write-up):

Descriptives: Mean burnout = 2.62 (SD = 0.71). By cohort: First M = 2.50 (SD = 0.58), Second M = 2.21 (SD = 0.56), Final M = 3.06 (SD = 0.64). Mean social support = 4.78 (SD = 0.80). Mean PSQI = 7.43 (SD = 2.42).

Correlations: Burnout correlated negatively with support (r = −.50, p < .001) and positively with sleep problems (r = +.43, p < .001). Support and sleep were weakly negatively correlated (r = −.08, p = .37).

One-way ANOVA: F(2, 117) = 38.94, p < .001, η² = .40. Tukey HSD: Second < First, p = .004, mean difference = −0.29; Final > First, p < .001, mean difference = +0.56; Final > Second, p < .001, mean difference = +0.85.

Multiple regression: F(2, 117) = 29.31, p < .001, R² = .334, R²_adj = .323. Support: b = −0.271, SE = 0.037, t(117) = −7.32, p < .001. Sleep: b = 0.082, SE = 0.013, t(117) = 6.47, p < .001.

Common Reporting Errors to Avoid

  • Writing "p = .000" — use "p < .001"
  • Omitting effect sizes — η², Cohen's d, R² are required
  • Writing "there was no significant difference" when the test simply did not reach p < .05 — this conflates absence of evidence with evidence of absence
  • Over-interpreting direction: "support protected against burnout" implies a mechanism the cross-sectional data cannot establish
  • Reporting results before assumption checks — assumption violations that were addressed must be reported

Limitations of This Study

A critical evaluation must address: (1) cross-sectional design — correlations and regression coefficients cannot establish causal direction; (2) self-report bias — burnout, support, and sleep are all self-reported, and common method variance may inflate correlations; (3) convenience sample — 120 students from one institution limits generalisability; (4) confounders — variables not measured (e.g., financial stress, course difficulty, pre-existing mental health conditions) may explain the relationships observed; (5) effect sizes — while η² = .40 for year group is large, the regression explains only 33% of burnout variance, leaving substantial unexplained variance attributable to unmeasured factors.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen projects the R output from 4b alongside a blank document. 'Numbers do not speak for themselves. A results section is not a printout — it is a translation. Every statistic requires a sentence that states what it means in the context of the research question.'

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Start with descriptives. You must report means and SDs before any inferential test — a reader needs to know the scale of the variables. Then the ANOVA: state the test statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, and eta-squared. Don't just say 'the result was significant.' Report F(2, 117) = 38.94, p < .001, η² = .40.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Then Tukey: which specific groups differ, by how much, and at what adjusted p-value. Then regression: report the overall model F and R², then each predictor's b, SE, t, and p. Tell the reader what b = −0.27 means in plain language: for each additional point of social support, burnout is predicted to decrease by 0.27 points, controlling for sleep quality.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: The critical evaluation is where the 1:1 student separates from the 2:1. Anyone can report statistics. Explaining why this cross-sectional study cannot establish that increasing social support will reduce burnout — and what design would be needed to establish that — is the intellectual work that distinguishes a scientist from a calculator.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Using the numerical results provided in the explanation above, write a complete APA 7 results section covering the capstone analyses. Your response should be structured as follows:

  1. Preliminary analyses: Report descriptive statistics (M, SD) for burnout, social support, and sleep quality. Report the key inter-correlations with r values and p-values.
  2. Year group differences in burnout (ANOVA): Report F, df, p, and η². Then report Tukey HSD results for each pairwise comparison.
  3. Predictors of burnout (multiple regression): Report the overall model (F, df, p, R², R²_adj), then each predictor (b, SE, t, p) with a plain-language interpretation of the slope.

Aim for 250–350 words. Write in formal academic prose as if submitting to a peer-reviewed journal. Do not interpret, theorise, or compare to other literature — that belongs in the discussion section.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Preliminary analyses. Descriptive statistics are reported in Table 1. Mean academic burnout was 2.62 (SD = 0.71) across the full sample. Social support (M = 4.78, SD = 0.80) correlated negatively with burnout, r(118) = −.50, p < .001, and sleep problems (PSQI; M = 7.43, SD = 2.42) correlated positively with burnout, r(118) = .43, p < .001. Social support and sleep problems were not significantly correlated, r(118) = −.08, p = .37, indicating low multicollinearity between predictors.

Year group differences in burnout. A one-way ANOVA revealed a significant effect of cohort on burnout, F(2, 117) = 38.94, p < .001, η² = .40. Tukey HSD post-hoc tests indicated that second-year students (M = 2.21, SD = 0.56) reported significantly lower burnout than first-year students (M = 2.50, SD = 0.58), mean difference = 0.29, p = .004. Final-year students (M = 3.06, SD = 0.64) reported significantly higher burnout than both first-year students, mean difference = 0.56, p < .001, and second-year students, mean difference = 0.85, p < .001.

Predictors of burnout. Multiple regression was used to examine whether social support and sleep quality independently predicted burnout. The overall model was significant, F(2, 117) = 29.31, p < .001, R² = .334, R²_adj = .323, indicating that social support and sleep quality together explained 32.3% of variance in burnout. Social support was a significant negative predictor, b = −0.27, SE = 0.04, t(117) = −7.32, p < .001: for each additional point of social support (on the 1–7 MSPSS scale), burnout was predicted to decrease by 0.27 points, holding sleep quality constant. Sleep problems were a significant positive predictor, b = 0.08, SE = 0.01, t(117) = 6.47, p < .001: for each additional PSQI point (indicating worse sleep), burnout was predicted to increase by 0.08 points, holding social support constant.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Write a critical evaluation of the capstone study's design and findings. Your evaluation should address:

  1. Two specific threats to internal validity — reasons why the observed associations may not reflect causal relationships
  2. One threat to external validity — a limitation in how far the findings can be generalised
  3. A proposed improved design that would address at least one of the limitations you identified — be specific about the design type, sample, and measures
  4. A brief statement of what the findings do establish, stated precisely without overinterpretation

Aim for 200–280 words. No scaffolding is provided.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: A junior colleague says: "Our regression shows social support predicts burnout, so we should recommend that universities improve students' social support networks to reduce burnout." What is right and what is wrong with this conclusion? Explain the distinction between association and causation in plain language and describe what evidence would be needed to justify the policy recommendation.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
The capstone study's cross-sectional design is its most significant internal validity limitation. Because social support, sleep quality, and burnout were all measured at the same time point, the direction of causality cannot be established. Two specific threats are: first, reverse causation — high burnout may itself cause poor sleep and withdrawal from social relationships, meaning the observed correlations could reflect burnout causing low support and poor sleep rather than the reverse; second, common method variance — all variables were self-reported, and shared method factors (mood at time of survey, response style) may inflate the correlations between them independently of their true relationships.

The most significant external validity limitation is the convenience sample: 120 students from a single institution, likely recruited through department participant pools, are not representative of university students generally. Students in different disciplines, institution types, or countries may show substantially different burnout patterns, limiting generalisability.

An improved design would be a longitudinal panel study: measuring social support, sleep, and burnout at three time points (start of year, mid-year, end of year) using the same students. This would allow cross-lagged panel analysis — testing whether Time 1 social support predicts Time 2 burnout after controlling for Time 1 burnout (and vice versa), separating bidirectional effects. Including multiple institutions across different demographics would address external validity.

What this study does establish, precisely: in this sample of 120 students, self-reported social support and sleep quality were significantly associated with self-reported burnout in the expected directions. Social support and sleep together accounted for 32% of variance in burnout. Final-year students reported higher burnout than first- or second-year students. These are descriptive facts about associations in one cross-sectional dataset, not causal claims about mechanisms.

rabbitHoleTerms.definition: Spurious covariance between variables that arises because they were all measured using the same method (typically self-report), rather than reflecting genuine relationships between constructs. Can inflate correlations among self-reported psychological measures and is a significant limitation of cross-sectional survey research.

A longitudinal analytical approach measuring variables at two or more time points and examining whether Variable A at Time 1 predicts Variable B at Time 2 (and vice versa), after controlling for stability in each variable. Allows directional inference about associations that purely cross-sectional designs cannot provide.

Writing the results section requires precision about what evidence shows versus what it implies. A cross-sectional correlation establishes co-variation, not causation; a significant regression coefficient establishes a predictive relationship in the sample, not a mechanism. Overstating findings is a form of scientific dishonesty, even if unintentional.

questions.questionHtml: A results section states: "Social support significantly protected students from burnout (b = −0.27, p < .001), demonstrating that improving support networks will reduce academic burnout." Which specific claim in this sentence goes beyond what the data establish?
options: "significantly" — the p-value threshold is arbitrary
"b = −0.27" — effect sizes should not be reported in the results section
"will reduce academic burnout" — the cross-sectional regression establishes association, not causal efficacy; an intervention study would be needed to establish this claim
"protected students" — protection implies causation and is inappropriate language
questions.correctAnswer: "will reduce academic burnout" — the cross-sectional regression establishes association, not causal efficacy; an intervention study would be needed to establish this claim
questions.explanationHtml: "Will reduce" implies a causal effect of an intervention — something a cross-sectional regression cannot establish. The analysis shows that self-reported social support is associated with lower self-reported burnout in this sample; it does not show that externally increasing social support would reduce burnout, which would require an experimental design. "Protected" in the first clause is also a slightly causal framing, but "will reduce" is the clearest overreach. Writing results sections requires disciplined avoidance of causal language from associational evidence.

questions.questionHtml: Writing up the ANOVA results, a student writes: "There was no significant difference in burnout between first- and second-year students (p = .004)." What is wrong with this sentence?
options: Nothing — p = .004 is not significant at the conventional .05 threshold
The sentence contradicts itself: p = .004 is significant (p < .05), not non-significant
The student should have reported t not F for pairwise comparisons
The sentence is missing the mean difference and effect size
questions.correctAnswer: The sentence contradicts itself: p = .004 is significant (p < .05), not non-significant
questions.explanationHtml: p = .004 is well below the conventional α = .05 threshold, meaning the null hypothesis of no difference is rejected — the comparison IS significant. The student has either misread their output or confused the direction. The correct statement would be: "First-year students reported significantly higher burnout than second-year students (mean difference = 0.29, p = .004)." Always match your verbal description to the numerical result, and verify which direction the effect goes (which group is higher).

questions.questionHtml: True or False: A limitation that should always be reported in the discussion section of a cross-sectional study is that the design prevents causal conclusions, even if the correlational findings are statistically robust.
questions.explanationHtml: The cross-sectional design limitation is not optional to report — it is fundamental. No matter how strong or statistically significant the associations, a cross-sectional study cannot rule out reverse causation, third-variable confounding, or common method variance. A results section that does not acknowledge this in the limitations section of the discussion is scientifically incomplete. This is not a minor technical caveat but a core constraint on the inferential weight the findings can carry.

questions.questionHtml: In an APA 7 results section, when a p-value from R is reported as "< 2.2e-16", how should this be written?
questions.explanationHtml: APA 7 style rounds p-values to three decimal places. When the exact p-value is smaller than .001, report it as p < .001 — never as p = .000 (which is numerically incorrect; the probability is not literally zero) and never as a scientific notation value from R output (which is not reader-friendly and implies false precision). If the journal requires exact p-values and the software cannot display them beyond a threshold, p < .001 is the appropriate convention.
